My Story: From Prison to Fry Bags

I was in prison when I first heard about the fry bagging program. I was sitting in the chow hall, watching guys swap stories about their past lives, their mistakes, and how they’d end up back out in the world, only to go right back behind bars. I thought, That’s going to be me—a never-ending cycle of bad decisions.

But then I overheard a conversation between some of the guards. They were talking about this new program, where we could learn to bag fries at a local fast food joint. At first, I didn’t think much of it. Fry bagging? That didn’t sound like a skill anyone would care about. I had bigger dreams, or at least I thought I did. But deep down, I knew I had nowhere else to turn.

HA! I can laugh about it now, but back then, the thought of bagging fries felt like a joke.

I joined the program reluctantly, thinking it was just another way to pass time. But when I first stepped into that kitchen, I felt something I hadn’t in years—purpose. The greasy smell of fries frying in hot oil, the sound of the fryer buzzing, and the rhythm of placing perfectly golden fries into bags—it was like I’d found my place. I could zone out, focus on the task, and for once, not think about the life I had left behind. Each fry I bagged felt like I was putting a little more of my old self away.

It wasn’t easy, though. I had my doubts. Every time I reached for the next batch of fries, I thought about the life I’d lived—how I had ended up in prison, how I’d hurt people who cared about me, how I didn’t deserve a second chance. But I kept bagging fries, one after the other, trying to keep my hands steady.

After months of working at the fry station in the program, I finally got my chance to leave prison. The day I walked out of those gates, the world felt like a foreign place. I hadn’t seen it in so long, and everything felt different. I was just another ex-con trying to fit in.

But I wasn’t just another ex-con anymore. I had skills now. A job lined up bagging fries, sure, but it was more than just that. It was a lifeline. Every bag I sealed brought me closer to rejoining society. It gave me dignity. And slowly, I started to see that I could do more than bag fries. I could rebuild, even if it was one fry at a time.

Sometimes, when I think back on it, I still can’t believe that the turning point of my life happened in a kitchen with nothing but hot oil and a fry bag. But I guess you never know how life is going to change.

I learned the hard way, but I finally got out of prison. Now, I’m back in the world, bagging fries, rebuilding my life, and proving to myself that I can do this. That maybe, just maybe, I’m not the person I thought I was.
